title: Beloved
events_chronological: Sethe is brought as a girl to a Kentucky farm and chooses Halle from among the men there.
Baby Suggs is bought out of slavery by Halle's extra labour and settles in a house outside Cincinnati.
A new owner the slaves call schoolteacher arrives at the farm and begins measuring them and writing them up in a book.
Sethe overhears schoolteacher telling his nephews to list her animal characteristics on one side of the page and her human ones on the other.
The men at the farm lay a plan to run, and the plan collapses.
Schoolteacher's nephews hold Sethe down in the barn and take her milk while Halle watches from the loft and loses his mind.
Sethe, pregnant and beaten, walks north alone, and a white girl called Amy Denver delivers her baby in a boat.
Sethe reaches the house and has twenty-eight days of freedom, and Baby Suggs holds a feast for ninety people.
Schoolteacher comes to the house to take Sethe and the children back.
Sethe carries the children into the woodshed and cuts her elder daughter's throat with a handsaw.
Sethe is jailed and released, Baby Suggs takes to her bed and dies, and the neighbours stop coming to the house.
Sethe's two sons run away from a house haunted by the dead baby.
Paul D, one of the men from the farm, arrives after eighteen years and drives the ghost out of the house.
A young woman calling herself Beloved walks out of the water and comes to live with them.
Paul D is moved out of the house room by room and is finally taken to bed by Beloved in the shed.
Stamp Paid shows Paul D the newspaper cutting about the killing, and Paul D leaves.
Beloved swells and consumes Sethe, until thirty women come into the yard and sing until she is gone.
syuzhet_notes: The novel withholds the killing and approaches it repeatedly from different directions, so the same afternoon is entered five or six times before it is completed. Past and present interrupt each other mid-sentence with no marker.
fabula_notes: The chronology is recoverable from the ages of the children and from the dated newspaper cutting, though the prose never sets it out in order.
